cases.prompt:
TASK: questions

You are testing whether a developer understands the ARCHITECTURE of the repository https://github.com/acme/shop
at commit 0123456789ab: what each unit is for, the decisions that shaped it, and what
those decisions mean for the rest of the system. Questions climb a ladder of five levels, and a
developer is asked a level only once they have shown the levels above it. Each unit below
names the level to ask it at. Write 3 question(s) for each unit, every one at exactly
that unit's level, and return that level with each question.

The ladder:
1. purpose and placement: asks what the unit is for, or one consequence of its place in the system, answerable in a sentence. May name nothing from the code: components by their role, in plain language.
   Shape: "What job does <the part that does X> do for the rest of the system?"
2. decision and alternatives: asks what was chosen, what was rejected and what constraint forced the choice. May name nothing from the code.
   Shape: "<X> was chosen over <Y>. What constraint made that the better choice here?"
3. consequence across units: asks what else in the system would have to change if the decision were reversed or replaced by an alternative. May name nothing from the code.
   Shape: "If <the decision> were replaced by <the alternative>, what is the first other part of the system that would have to change?"
4. behaviour under failure: asks module-level edge cases and failure modes: what happens when a part fails, times out, gets empty input or runs twice. May name a file or a component, but no code (no function, class or variable names).
   Shape: "What does the user see when <a component> fails halfway through <an operation>?"
5. implementation: asks code paths and specific functions: what a given piece of code does and why. May name anything: files, functions, variables, code.
   Shape: "If you removed <a specific call or handler>, what would happen when <an event>?"

Every question has exactly one part and asks for exactly one fact: one question
mark, no second question joined on with "and what", "and which" or a semicolon, no second
sentence after it, and never a request to list, enumerate or name several things ("which other
parts ...", "name the ..."). A level 1 question asks what the unit is for, or one consequence of
its place in the system, and a developer who knows the answer can give it in one sentence. If a
unit has several things worth asking, ask the most important one.

Levels 1, 2 and 3 test the architecture, not the code. A question at these
levels must not name any function, method, class, variable, constant, file, directory,
module, endpoint or configuration key of this repository, and must not quote or paraphrase a
line or block of code. Name components by their role, in plain language ("the part that
streams replies to the browser", "the check that a user may open the admin pages"), as a
colleague would at a whiteboard. It may name an external technology, service or library
the decision is about (a database, a hosting platform, a model provider). Ask about the
unit's main decision and its place in the system, not its most specific consequence: a
developer who understands the shape of the system should be able to answer without opening a
file. A level 4 question may name a file or a component, but no code. A level 5 question may
name anything.

Some units carry the orientation the developer has just read: what the unit is for, its
decision and alternatives, where it lives and who shaped it. A level 1 question on such a
unit must not be answerable by copying a sentence of that text: ask one consequence that
follows from it, such as what a user would notice first if the unit stopped working, or why
it has to run before or after one named step of a request.

Every question must have an answer the code (or the cited commits) determines, so it can be
graded objectively. Avoid trivia (exact names, line counts, versions) at every level. You cannot open files: the code reaches you as the excerpts at the end,
taken from the repository at that commit, with the unit descriptions and the commit subjects
given; verify every reference answer against them. Cite the files you relied on in
`evidence`, each as `path` or `path:start-end`. The reference answer says what a correct answer must contain, and the developer reads it
right after a miss, so it teaches: at levels 1-3 it is at most two sentences of plain
language with no identifiers (the files go in `evidence`); at levels 4-5 at most three
sentences, and it may name files and functions. With each question give `variants`: two more
phrasings of the same question, each one part, asking the same fact, so the reference answer
fits all three.

Answer by calling the tool `submit` once, with every question.
